title: THE GUNSHOTS STOPPED IN ZAMBOANGA—BUT THERE IS A QUESTION STILL ECHOING THROUGH EVERY HOME
paragraphs: THE GUNSHOTS STOPPED IN ZAMBOANGA—BUT THERE IS A QUESTION STILL ECHOING THROUGH EVERY HOME

After the Ateneo de Zamboanga school shooting, perhaps the question Christians must ask is not merely, “How could this happen?” but something far more uncomfortable: “Who around us is silently falling apart while everybody assumes they are okay?”
A child went to school.
Another child went to school.
Parents expected classrooms, notebooks, conversations, assignments, ordinary complaints about an ordinary day.
Then gunfire shattered the ordinary.

On August 18, 2026, violence erupted at the Junior High School campus of Ateneo de Zamboanga University in Zamboanga City. Two minors died, including the student authorities identified as responsible for the attack, and others were injured. Authorities say portions of the violence were livestreamed. Investigators have been examining how the firearms were obtained and brought onto the campus, what may have contributed to the attack, and what safeguards could prevent another tragedy.

Some details reported during the first days have conflicted, as often happens during rapidly developing investigations involving minors. So we should resist the temptation to turn uncertain details into certainty.
But one fact requires no speculation.
Two children are dead.
Families are grieving.
Students heard sounds no child should have to hear at school.
And somewhere tonight, there are parents looking at their children differently.
Maybe holding them a little longer.
Maybe wondering what happens inside their minds after the bedroom door closes.
Maybe asking a question they never thought they would have to ask:
Do I really know what my child is carrying inside?
Because some wounds do not bleed where anyone can see them.
Some children laugh while hurting.
Some adults do too.
Some people sit beside us in classrooms, churches, offices, jeepneys, dinner tables and Sunday services carrying wars nobody else knows are happening.
And this is where the tragedy in Zamboanga must become more than another headline we consume before scrolling to something else.
We must not sensationalize the dead.
We must not endlessly circulate graphic footage.
We must not turn traumatized children into entertainment.
We must not pretend to know motives investigators themselves are still trying to establish.
And Christians especially must resist another temptation:
giving a simple spiritual explanation to a complicated human tragedy.
Jesus never taught us to look at suffering from a comfortable distance and congratulate ourselves for having an explanation.
He taught us to come near.
There is a tiny Greek word in the New Testament that reveals something breathtaking about the heart of Christ.
ἐσπλαγχνίσθη — esplanchnisthē.
It comes from σπλαγχνίζομαι — splagchnizomai.
Our English Bibles often translate it, “He had compassion.”
But the word is visceral.
It speaks of being moved in the deepest inward parts of a person.
When Jesus saw suffering, He was not merely intellectually concerned.
He was moved.
When Matthew 9:36 says Jesus saw the crowds and had compassion on them, the Greek text says:
ἰδὼν δὲ τοὺς ὄχλους ἐσπλαγχνίσθη περὶ αὐτῶν
Seeing the crowds, He was moved with compassion for them.
Why?
Because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.
That is where Christians should stand after Zamboanga.
Not above the grieving.
Beside them.
Not diagnosing people we never knew.
Weeping with people whose worlds have changed.
Not asking first, “Whose side am I supposed to take?”
But:
“Jesus, teach us to see people before their hidden pain becomes catastrophe.”
Because there was a victim whose life mattered.
There are wounded people whose lives matter.
There are classmates and teachers whose trauma matters.
There are parents whose grief matters.
And even when someone commits terrible violence, Christians cannot abandon the biblical truth that human beings are more than content, statistics, villains or headlines.
Human beings bear the image of God.
Genesis 1:27 says:
בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים — b’tselem Elohim.
“In the image of God.”
That does not excuse evil.
Christian compassion never requires pretending evil is good.
Murder is evil.
Violence is evil.
Taking innocent life violates the sacred dignity God gives human beings.
But Scripture forces us to hold another uncomfortable truth beside that one.
Every human heart needs redemption.
Including ours.
Perhaps that is why this story is so frightening.
We desperately want evil to belong exclusively to “those people.”
The dangerous people.
The disturbed people.
The people somewhere outside our homes and churches.
Then Jesus says something devastating:

“For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts…”
—Mark 7:21
Jesus locates humanity's deepest crisis somewhere security cameras cannot reach.
The human heart.
That does not mean security is unnecessary.
It does not mean firearm safeguards are unnecessary.
It does not mean schools, parents, authorities and communities should ignore warning signs, online influences, bullying, isolation, threats or emotional distress.
Quite the opposite.
Love pays attention.
Love protects.
Love intervenes.
Love asks difficult questions before funerals force us to ask them.
But Christianity says something even deeper.
Humanity does not merely need better circumstances.
Humanity needs reconciliation with God.
We need Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this has been hiding something too.
Not a weapon.
Pain.
Rage.
Shame.
A secret addiction.
Bitterness.
Thoughts you are terrified to tell anyone about.
A wound you keep disguising with jokes.
Maybe everyone thinks you are okay.
You know you aren't.
Please hear this:
Do not wait until your pain chooses your next action for you.
Tell someone.
Tell your parents.
Tell someone trustworthy.
Tell a pastor who will actually listen.
Tell a counselor.
Tell someone who can help keep you and other people safe.
And tell Jesus the truth.
Not the religious version.
The truth.
“I am angry.”
“I am jealous.”
“I hate what happened to me.”
“I don't know what I'm becoming.”
“Lord, help me.”
Christianity was never built upon pretending broken people were already whole.
It was built around a cross where sinners could finally stop pretending.
The Greek word translated “repent” is μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite, from μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It carries the sense of changing one's mind, turning, reconsidering one's direction.
Jesus begins His public proclamation in Mark 1:15 with a summons:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
Repentance is not God standing over shattered people shouting, “Become respectable.”
It is the King calling rebels home.
Turn around.
Come back.
Put down what is destroying you.
Stop feeding the darkness.
Stop rehearsing revenge.
Stop hiding.
Come into the light.
And there, standing in the light, is not a Savior shocked by what He discovers.
There is Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Still calling sinners.
The Gospel does not say your darkest chapter never happened.
It says your darkest chapter does not have to write your final sentence.
That is why the cross remains the greatest scandal of grace history has ever witnessed.
Jesus did not die because humanity was basically fine.
He died because sin is devastatingly real.
Yet the same cross declaring the horror of sin declares something else:
mercy is real too.
χάρις — charis.
Grace.
Undeserved favor.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The ashamed can come home.
The spiritually dead can live.
The violent heart can be transformed.
The bitter heart can become tender.
The addicted can seek freedom.
The proud can kneel.
The hiding can step into light.
Not because Christianity offers motivational language.
Because Jesus Christ lives.
Maybe that is the word somebody desperately needs tonight.
Come into the light before darkness convinces you there is nowhere left to go.
And parents...
please look up from your phones.
Children...
please look up from yours.
Families...
talk.
Not only when something goes wrong.
Ask the uncomfortable question.
“How are you really?”
Then survive the silence long enough to hear the answer.
Churches, become places where struggling young people can tell the truth without immediately becoming gossip.
Pastors, preach holiness without making wounded people terrified to admit they are wounded.
Christians, stop assuming the quiet person is okay because they smiled during worship.
Teachers, keep noticing.
Friends, keep checking.
And if someone tells you they may harm themselves or somebody else, do not keep that information secret merely because they asked you to.
Get responsible adults and emergency professionals involved immediately.
Sometimes love sounds like prayer.
Sometimes love sounds like listening.
And sometimes love sounds like:
“I care about you too much to leave you alone with this.”
There is another Greek sentence Christians should carry into moments like this.
Romans 12:15:
κλαίειν μετὰ κλαιόντων
“Weep with those who weep.”
Notice what Paul does not say.
Exploit those who weep.
Photograph those who weep.
Turn those who weep into arguments.
He says:
Weep.
So before you share footage from Zamboanga, ask whether sharing it protects dignity or feeds curiosity.
Before repeating an allegation, ask whether it has actually been established.
Before turning minors into permanent internet identities attached to the worst day imaginable, remember that families are grieving behind these headlines.
Share truth.
Share compassion.
Share resources that may help someone.
But don't make another person's trauma your entertainment.
And maybe this article should not end with Zamboanga at all.
Maybe it should end in your house.
With one bedroom door.
One conversation.
One apology.
One phone call.
One prayer.
One father finally saying, “Son, talk to me.”
One mother finally saying, “You don't have to hide this from me.”
One teenager finally whispering, “I need help.”
One Christian finally confessing, “Jesus, I have been feeding something inside me that needs to die.”
One sinner discovering that the door of grace is still open.
Not because comments save anybody.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession breaks isolation, testimony reminds another person that they are not alone, and one honest sentence gives someone else permission to finally speak.
Come back to it when anger tells you revenge is strength.
Come back when shame tells you hiding is safer.
Come back when despair tells you your story is finished.
We want this community to remain a place for daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
It is not purchasing God's favor.
It does not make you more loved by God.
You do not buy blessing, salvation or spiritual status.
The Gospel cannot be bought.

But voluntary generosity can help Gospel-centered teaching travel farther. Your sharing can put biblical truth in front of someone we may never meet. Your support can help us keep creating resources intended to point wounded, wandering and searching people toward Jesus.
whether you buy anything or never do...
do something infinitely more important.
Go to Jesus.
Then go check on somebody.
Listen before judging.
Protect before posting.
Pray before speculating.
Repent where the Holy Spirit exposes you.
Forgive where Christ commands you.
Seek help where darkness has become dangerous.
And remember the families in Zamboanga who now have to live beyond a morning they would give anything to undo.
A headline will eventually disappear from our feeds.
Their grief will not.
May the Church still be there when everybody else has scrolled away.
May we become people who notice suffering before it becomes spectacle.
May parents listen.
May children speak.
May churches become safe places for truth.
May responsible authorities pursue truth and meaningful protection.
May wounded minds find compassionate help.
May those harboring hatred surrender it before hatred demands a price that can never be refunded.
And above everything...
may sinners discover that there is still a blood-stained cross, an empty tomb, and a Savior whose invitation remains open.
Because perhaps the most terrifying lie darkness whispers is:
“It is too late for you.”
The Gospel answers:
Jesus is still calling you home.
Because after the screaming stops...
after the cameras leave...
after the hashtags disappear...
there will still be human hearts needing somebody to notice them.
And sometimes the person standing one conversation away from the edge looks completely ordinary.
